text.american: English has no throaty ch, and it spells a k sound with ch in “Christ”, “chorus” and “character”, so a reader says χ as k. It is never k. Before α, ο, ω, ου or a consonant it is the throaty ch of “chutzpah”: the back of the tongue comes close to the roof of the mouth and the air rubs through. Before an e or i sound (ε, αι, η, ι, υ, ει, οι) it moves forward and softens, to the h of “huge” said with a hiss.
text.british: Standard English has no throaty ch, and it spells a k sound with ch in “Christ”, “chorus” and “character”, so a reader says χ as k. It is never k. Before α, ο, ω, ου or a consonant it is the ch of Scottish “loch”, never “lock”: the back of the tongue comes close to the roof of the mouth and the air rubs through. Before an e or i sound (ε, αι, η, ι, υ, ει, οι) it moves forward and softens, to the h of “huge” said with a hiss.

text.american: Say a k slowly, and stop the back of the tongue just before it touches: let the air rub through the narrow gap, as at the start of “chutzpah”. That is χ. For the soft one, say “huge” and hold the h until it hisses: that is χ before e and i, as in ἔχει.
text.british: Say “loch” the Scottish way and hold the end: the air rubs through a narrow gap at the back of the mouth. That is χ. For the soft one, say “huge” and hold the h until it hisses: that is χ before e and i, as in ἔχει.

steps.text: Listen to the throaty χ before α, ο and ρ in χαρά, ἔχομεν and χριστοῦ, and to the soft one before an e or i sound in ἔχει, χεῖρες and ἀρχῆς. Never a k.

In the first three pairs χ stands against κ, the sound an English reader puts in its place: for χ the tongue comes close and stops there. In the last it stands against nothing at all: do not let the soft χ fade to a breath.
Say each word after the voice. If you hear a k, the tongue touched: let it come close and stop there. Before e and i, move it forward, to the hissed h of “huge”.
This verse turns on one word, said four times, each χ marked: the throaty χ of ἔχων and the soft χ of ἔχει. Hear it, then say it, keeping the two apart.
